sections.heading: Destination Snapshot
sections.body: Gorge de la Jonte is a Causses gorge destination for limestone and dolomite multi-pitch climbing: long positions, mixed protection styles and a quieter feel than the better-known Tarn.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body:
The Jonte sits in southern France's gorge country, with big faces, exposed positions and a climbing style that asks for judgement as well as fitness.

It is not just a sport-crag stop. Most routes are multi-pitch, with both traditional and sport protection. That makes it a strong venue for teams that want longer days and real route management.

sections.heading: History
sections.body:
The Jonte’s reputation is tied to gorge climbing: big air, long limestone and dolomite faces, and routes that feel more adventurous than roadside single-pitch climbing.

Its quieter character is part of the appeal. The best trips keep the rhythm measured: early starts, clear route choice, enough water and no rush on descents.

sections.heading: Rock and Style
sections.body:
The rock is limestone and dolomite, with slabs, pockets, overhangs and long featured walls. Expect multi-pitch movement rather than short gym-style burns.

Protection varies by route. Some climbing is sport-equipped, some is more traditional in character, and every team should check the exact line before committing.

sections.heading: Who Is It For
sections.body:
The Jonte suits experienced roped climbers who are comfortable with multi-pitch systems, exposure and route finding. Sport climbers can enjoy it if they already have the rope skills for longer routes.

It is not the best venue for a first outdoor lead unless the day is guided or kept very conservative.

sections.heading: Grades and Scale
sections.body:
The Jonte has about 300 mostly multi-pitch routes from 5b to 8b+. That range allows moderate and advanced teams to build a week, but route length and protection style should guide choices as much as grade.

Use the grade range as an overview, then plan from a current topo.

sections.heading: Season
sections.body:
The Jonte can work across the year, but gorge conditions still matter. Sun, wind, rain and seasonal restrictions can make one wall sensible and another poor.

Keep the season flexible and confirm current local access before committing to a sector.

sections.heading: Gear
sections.body:
Bring multi-pitch equipment, helmets and a rack matched to the exact route. For some lines that may mean a sport rack; for others, additional traditional gear may be appropriate.

Carry enough water and layers for a long day in the gorge, not just the climbing time.

sections.heading: Getting There
sections.body:
A car is the practical way to handle the Jonte. The destination is a gorge area with scattered starts, parking and descent logistics.

Plan approaches and exits before leaving the car, especially if climbing a longer route.

sections.heading: Stay and Eat
sections.body:
Campsites and guesthouse-style accommodation are the practical lodging categories to plan around. Confirm specific places before booking.

A good base is one that makes early starts, food supplies and rest-day access straightforward.

sections.heading: Rest Days
sections.body: Rest days can stay in the gorge landscape: walking, viewpoints, river time and nearby villages. If weather or access rules close one objective, the broader Causses area still gives useful non-climbing options.

sections.heading: Tips and Ethics
sections.body:
Choose routes by team efficiency, not only by grade. Multi-pitch days in the Jonte need time for approach, climbing, descent and weather changes.

Check current access information, especially for nature restrictions, before choosing sectors.

sections.heading: Safety
sections.body:
Treat the Jonte as a multi-pitch venue. Helmets, descent knowledge, rope management and conservative timing matter.

Rockfall, exposure and route-finding errors carry bigger consequences than at a single-pitch crag. Start early and keep margins.

sections.heading: FAQ
sections.body:
What style is the Jonte? Mostly multi-pitch limestone and dolomite, with both sport and traditional protection.

What grades are covered? The useful spread runs from mid-grade classics into hard routes across about 300 lines.

Do I need a car? Yes, it is the practical option.
